podcast.title: "Minstrily Behaviours" Criticism
podcast.body: In their early years, Deek Watson, performing under the name Dice Vastus in his coffee pot group, was criticized in early reviews of The Ink Spots for "eye rolling, hand waving, and other minstrily behaviours." This often drew disapproval from Black reviewers who felt it perpetuated negative stereotypes. "Many early reviews of the ink spots criticised him for eye rolling, hand waving, and other minstrily behaviours, which many black reviewers at the time considered brought black people into this repute."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Top and Bottom" Formula Development
podcast.body: Bill Kenny, an inspired arranger, refined Hoppy Jones' occasional spoken vocals into a hit formula. This arrangement started with an acoustic guitar figure, followed by Kenny's high-tenor lead vocal, then Hoppy Jones speaking the entire lyrics in his deep bass voice, and finally Kenny singing the last line. This formula was first used in the studio on "If I Didn't Care" and was consistently applied to subsequent hits. "He refined the idea of Hoppy's spoken vocals, and came up with a hit formula, which they would use over and over again."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Backing Band for Bill Doggett
podcast.body: The Ink Spots' backing band later included Bill Doggett, who joined them after having worked with Lucky Millinder. "He'd worked with Bill Doggett before Doggett went off to join the ink spots backing band."

podcast.title: Bill Doggett's Influence on Arrangements
podcast.body: In the mid-1940s, Bill Doggett was responsible for arranging many of The Ink Spots' songs, contributing to the consistent sound that defined their hits. "and in the mid-40s those songs were arranged by Bill Doggert."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Bill Kenny's Impact and "Top and Bottom" Formula
podcast.body: In 1936, 21-year-old high-tenor singer Bill Kenny joined the band after winning an amateur contest at the Savoy Ballroom, which was co-owned by The Ink Spots' manager, Mo Gale. Kenny's extraordinary vocals became the defining characteristic of their records, and he is credited with conceiving the "Top and Bottom" idea, transforming the band from an up-tempo jive act into a balladeering group. "Bill Kenny, a 21-year-old high-tener singer, won an amateur night contest at the Savoy Ballroom."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Bill Kenny's Post-Split Recordings
podcast.body: Following the split with Charlie Fouquet, Bill Kenny continued to make records under The Ink Spots name. These recordings maintained the classic Ink Spots sound, but notably lacked the deep bass spoken vocals of Hoppy Jones, who had passed away years prior. "Meanwhile, Bill Kenny was still making records as the ink spots, which still sounded like the old ink spots, minus Hoppy's bass vocal."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Charlie Fouquet's "New Ink Spots"
podcast.body: After parting with Bill Kenny in 1952, Charlie Fouquet began touring as "Charlie Fouquet's New Ink Spots," despite an earlier agreement that only Kenny's band could legally use the name. He later broke this agreement by performing simply as "The Ink Spots" and even briefly reunited with Deke Watson in his version of the group. "Fookeway would tour as Charlie Fookeway's new ink spots, except that Fookeway soon ended up breaking this agreement and just touring and recording as the ink spots."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Chart Dominance with Formula
podcast.body: The Ink Spots' "Top and Bottom" formula proved incredibly successful, selling tens of millions of records from approximately 1939 to the late 1940s. Many of their songs, including "I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire," reached the Top 10, with some even hitting number 1 on the pop charts, not just the R&B charts. "This was a formula that absolutely, undoubtedly worked. And when I say number 1 or top 10, I don't mean on the R&B charts. I mean number 1 on the pop charts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Collaborations with Ella Fitzgerald
podcast.body: When The Ink Spots were not touring, their members, including Bill Doggett, would perform with Ella Fitzgerald, who was also managed by Mo Gale. Fitzgerald also recorded a number of hit singles with the group, featuring Doggett on piano. "And indeed, during the end of Doggert's time with the ink spot, Fitzgerald recorded a number of hit singles with the group, which of course featured Doggert on the piano."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Consistent Hit-Making Formula
podcast.body: The Ink Spots had numerous hit singles throughout the 1940s, all of which sounded remarkably similar due to their adherence to their established formula. "They had hit after hit during the 40s with songs that all sound remarkably similar."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Deke Watson's Departure and First Legal Battle
podcast.body: Allegedly after Mo Gale gave Bill Kenny a pay rise while not extending it to Watson or Jones, Deke Watson quit the band to form his own version of The Ink Spots. This move, combined with Hoppy Jones' death, ignited a complex four-way legal battle involving Watson, Kenny, Charlie Fouquet (still in the army), and Mo Gale. "Deke Watson quit the band as a result of this, and went off to form his own ink spots."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Names and Beginnings
podcast.body: Before settling on The Ink Spots, members performed in various combinations under different names, including "Charlie and Jerry" (Fouquay and Daniels) and "King Jack and Jester" (or "King Jack and Jester's"). In their early years, they secured a video show on a local station as a fill-in for The Four Mills Brothers, who heavily influenced their initial sound. "Before they settled on calling themselves King Jack and Jester, or sometimes King Jack and Jester's."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: First Court Ruling on Band Name
podcast.body: The initial legal battle primarily favored Bill Kenny, ruling that no club could book an act called The Ink Spots unless Kenny was a member. However, Deke Watson and Charlie Fouquet retained a financial interest in the band, Mo Gale remained manager, and Fouquet was paid a regular salary during his army service. "The courts ruled that no club could book an act called the ink spots, which didn't have Bill Kenny in it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Formation from Coffee Pot Groups
podcast.body: The Ink Spots formed from musicians who had started their careers in "coffee pot groups," which were comprised of poor Black teenagers performing on street corners, using everyday items like kazoos and containers to imitate orchestral sounds. Original members Charlie Fouquay, Jerry Daniels, Deek Watson, and Happy Jones emerged from this background. "The ink spots formed out of people who'd started their careers in these groups."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Historical Precedent for "Fake" Bands
podcast.body: The situation with numerous "fake" Platters groups touring without original members was compared to a similar issue that plagued The Ink Spots, indicating a common problem in the music industry with band names. "There have been almost as many fake platters as they have fake ink spots."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Hoppy Jones' Illness and Death
podcast.body: Hoppy Jones, crucial to the "Top and Bottom" sound, became increasingly ill, missing more and more dates due to a series of brain hemorrhages. Tragically, after Deek Watson quit the band, Jones collapsed on stage and died, a pivotal moment that dissolved the original partnership and led to further legal battles. "But Hoppy Jones was growing ill and started missing more and more dates because of what turned out to be a series of brain hemorrhages."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence on Elvis Presley
podcast.body: The Ink Spots' song "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" was a favorite of a young Elvis Presley. In 1953, shortly after the band's final split, Presley chose to record his own version of the song as a gift for his mother when he walked into a Memphis recording studio to make his first single. "He wanted to make a record of himself singing as a gift for his mother, and he chose one of his favourite songs. That's when your heartakes begin, as one of the two tracks he would record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influence on Sam Cooke
podcast.body: Sam Cooke studied and learned from the vocal stylings of artists like Bill Kenny of The Ink Spots, contributing to his development into a versatile singer. "he was also learning from people like Jean Nortry or Bill Kenny of the Inc. Spots, and he was slowly developing into a singer who could do absolutely anything with his voice."

podcast.title: Intended Recipients of "Only You"
podcast.body: Book Ram had originally written "Only You" with the intention of passing it on to The Ink Spots, a group he had previously written for. However, he never got around to it, and his later claim that they had split up by then was inaccurate. "Only you was a song that Ram had written with the intention of passing it on to the ink spot."

podcast.title: Jerry Daniels' Illness and Departure
podcast.body: Jerry Daniels, who served as the band's main jive singer, became seriously ill from the stress of their performing schedule and was eventually hospitalized. His inability to continue touring led to a temporary reduction of the group to three members and necessitated a change in their lineup and sound. "Jerry Damules, their main jive singer, was getting seriously ill from the stress of the band's performing schedule, and eventually ended up hospitalised."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Last Original Member and Final Performance
podcast.body: Huey Long, who served as a temporary replacement for Charlie Fouquet for nine months in 1945, was the last actual Ink Spots member, dying at the age of 106 in 2009. The last known gig for any iteration of The Ink Spots that could be traced was in 2013, marking the long and complex end of their performing career. "The last actual ink spots member, Huey Long, who had been one of the temporary replacements for Charlie Fouquet in 1945 for nine months, died aged 106 in 2009."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Leadership Conflict and Hoppy Jones' Role
podcast.body: By 1944, deep personality conflicts emerged between Deek Watson, who saw himself as the leader for founding and naming the band, and Bill Kenny, who believed he was the leader due to his lead vocals and arranging skills. Hoppy Jones, having worked with Watson for years and holding an assured place with his spoken parts, acted as the peacemaker between the two. "Deke Watson and Bill Kenny never got on very well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Lineup Changes During Bill Doggett's Tenure
podcast.body: During Bill Doggett's two years with the group, he was part of the classic lineup and witnessed key personnel changes, including Charlie Fouquet being drafted and Deek Watson being fired. "He was with the group for two years, starting with the classic lineup of the group, and staying with them, through Charlie Fouquet being drafted, and Deek Watson being fired."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 50: "Honky Tonk", by Bill Doggett

podcast.title: Lineup Changes and Wartime Draft
podcast.body: The Ink Spots experienced a series of lineup changes due to personality conflicts, legal disputes, and deaths. In 1942, Charlie Fouquet was drafted into the army, leading to three years of replacements covering his part and marking the beginning of significant shifts in the band's personnel. "Four years after their career took off, in 1942 Charlie Fouquet was drafted, and that began a whole series of line-up shifts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lineups in the 1960s
podcast.body: Freddie Houston, whose vocal style was compared to Billy LeBvano, became the lead singer for one of the numerous lineups of The Ink Spots that toured during the 1960s. "who would go on to be the lead singer in one of the many ink spots line-ups touring in the 60s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Live Recording with Fouquet and Watson
podcast.body: One recording exists of a version of The Ink Spots featuring original members Charlie Fouquet and Deke Watson, alongside Jimmy Holmes and Harold Jackson, performing live at the Apollo. This brief reunion occurred before Watson was once again removed from Fouquet's band. "There's one recording of that version of the band, Jimmy Holmes, Charlie Fookeway, Deke Watson and Harold Jackson, live at the Apollo, before Watson was kicked out again."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Mo Gale's Management and Finances
podcast.body: Mo Gale, The Ink Spots' manager and co-owner of the Savoy Ballroom, managed other bands like Ella Fitzgerald and Lucky Millinder, enabling him to organize package tours and find easy replacements for ill or departing members. However, Gale notoriously took 60% of the band's earnings, leaving 40% to be split four ways among the members, leading to future conflicts. "Gale took 60 percent, while the eggspots got the other 40 between them, split four ways."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Most Popular Black Act of the 1940s
podcast.body: The Ink Spots were a vocal quartet who achieved significant fame, becoming the most popular Black act of the 1940s. "The Inc spots, if you don't remember, were a vocal quartet, who became the most popular Black Act of the 40s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Name Origin Controversy
podcast.body: Deek Watson claimed he suggested the name "The Ink Spots" after seeing drops of ink fall from a booking agent's pen. However, his bandmates, particularly Charlie and Happy, reacted negatively, interpreting it as another one of Watson's attempts to emphasize their race, comparing it to "Black dots" or "old black joes." "To me, it seemed like inspiration. That's it, I shouted. How about calling us the ink spots?"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Post-War Lineup and Subsequent Departures
podcast.body: After Charlie Fouquet returned from the war, a new lineup featuring Bill Kenny, his brother Herb Kenny, Fouquet, and Billy Bowen toured and recorded for several years. However, in 1952, Fouquet and Bill Kenny decided to part ways, leading to further disputes over the band's name. "Fouquet came back, and for a few years a new lineup of Bill Kenny and his brother Herb, Fouquet and Billy Bowen, Tordon recorded."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Proliferation of "The Ink Spots" Groups
podcast.body: As a direct result of the court ruling that dissolved legitimate ownership of the name, anyone could form a group and call themselves "The Ink Spots." This led to a proliferation of touring and recording groups, with up to 40 different "Ink Spots" acts performing at one point, often with tenuous or no direct connection to the original band. "At one point, there were up to 40 different ink spots groups touring, and many of them were recording too."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 6: "That's When Your Heartaches Begin" by the Ink Spots

podcast.title: Second Court Ruling and Name Dissolution
podcast.body: Faced with two competing versions of The Ink Spots, a second court case was initiated. Unexpectedly, the judge ruled that because The Ink Spots were a partnership and not a corporation, the partnership had legally dissolved upon Hoppy Jones' death a decade earlier. This meant that no one, neither surviving original members nor Bill Kenny, had a legitimate claim to the name, effectively making it public domain. "Instead, the ruling was one that no one had expected, and that no one wanted. You see, it turns out that the ink spots weren't a corporation. They were a partnership."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unique Vocal Formula
podcast.body: The group was known for its distinct and unique musical formula, centered around Bill Kenny's high tenor vocals and Hoppy Jones's characteristic low-spoken bass delivery. "and who stuck to a unique formula based around Bill Kenny's Hyg Tenor and Hoppy Jones's low-spoken base."
